paras: The lynching of William Cooper took place on the night of about August 18, 1885, when a mob went to the house of Cooper, a Black man, in the Seventeenth District of Madison County, Tennessee, and shot him dead. The mob also wounded Jack Allison, a young white man, who was expected to die, and no arrests had been made two days later.

According to a special dispatch from Jackson to the Memphis Daily Appeal, the trouble began a few weeks earlier, when Cooper chased his employer, James Whitenton, out of a field and that night went to Whitenton's house and called him out. The dispatch said that Cooper "made a motion as if to draw a pistol" and that Whitenton shot him several times, severely wounding him. As Cooper recovered, he reportedly threatened to kill Whitenton and all his family, and the correspondent wrote that "the whole community became aroused."

On the night of about August 18, a mob went to Cooper's house and fired several times, and five shots passed through his body, killing him instantly. In the shooting, Allison was struck in the arm and lungs by a load of buckshot fired by the mob, "either accidentally or through mistake," and the dispatch said he would die.

As of August 20 no arrests had been made, and the correspondent expressed the hope that matters would be settled "without further bloodshed." No report of an inquest, an arrest, or Allison's fate was found in the coverage.

The killing is known from a single dispatch, printed on the front page of the Memphis Daily Appeal on August 21, 1885, under the headline "A Negro Desperado Shot to Death by a Mob." The Appeal's correspondent described Cooper as "a desperate negro" who was "said to have killed one or two men" and presented the mobbing as the result of an aroused community, without naming any member of the mob. No coverage of the killing was found in other white papers or in the Black press.

reader.title: Lynching of William Cooper
bases: A mob went to William Cooper's house and shot him dead after the community 'became aroused' over his reported threats against his employer [A1].

A1 reports that a mob, acting without any legal authority, shot Cooper five times and killed him because he had reportedly threatened to kill his employer and the employer's family, the community having 'became aroused'; the mob's size is not given, but it is described as a mob and its action as a community response [A1].
The only report found is a special dispatch from Jackson to the Memphis Daily Appeal [A1]; no other white or Black paper was found carrying it.

a mob in the Seventeenth District, this county, went to the house of William Cooper, colored, and fired several times, five shots passing through his body, killing him instantly.
Jack Allison, a young white man, was also shot in the arm and lungs with a load of buckshot by the mob, either accidentally or through mistake, and will die.
